data.copy:
My daughter’s wedding should have been one of the happiest days of my life.

Instead, I was terrified.

Not because of the dress.
Not because of the speeches.
Not even because of the photos.

Because my ex-husband was bringing his new girlfriend.

And she is seven years older than our daughter.

Yes. Really.

When my daughter first told me, I laughed because I genuinely thought she was joking. Our daughter is 29. Which made his girlfriend 36.

I’m 58.

You do that math and suddenly every mirror in your house becomes cruel.

I know how ridiculous this sounds. I do.
But something happens to a woman after divorce — especially after 50.
You spend years rebuilding yourself. Learning how to exist alone. Learning how to feel okay again.
And then one day your ex walks into the room with someone young enough to still get carded at restaurants and every insecurity you thought you buried comes clawing back up.

I hadn’t worn foundation properly in almost four years.

Because every single one made me look older.

The moment makeup touched my skin, it settled into lines I didn’t even know I had. By midday it would separate around my mouth, cling to dry patches, turn orange around my chin.

I looked tired. Older. Heavy.

So eventually I gave up.

I became one of those women who says things like:
“Oh, I’m just not a makeup person anymore.”
“It’s fine, I don’t care.”

Meanwhile I absolutely cared.

Especially now.

Because this wasn’t just any event.
This was my daughter’s wedding.
There would be photographers everywhere. Videos. Close-ups. Family photos that would exist forever.

And standing somewhere in those photos would be my ex-husband’s thirty-something girlfriend with smooth glowing skin and collagen still naturally occurring in her face.

I know comparison is ugly.
But heartbreak at this age is ugly too.

So two weeks before the wedding, I did something I hadn’t done in years.

I've spent 19 years fixing athletes.

Runners.

Cyclists.

CrossFit competitors.

Weekend ski injuries.

My hardest patients aren't any of them.

My hardest patients are gardeners.

And I need to explain why because nobody else is going to.

My name is Scott.

I'm 44.

I'm a sports physical therapist in Fort Collins, Colorado.

I've been in practice since 2007.

I work with college runners, recreational cyclists, the local CrossFit box, a handful of semi-pro climbers.

I fix movement patterns for a living.

That's not the glamorous version of what I do.

The glamorous version is "sports rehab."

The real version is: somebody comes in moving wrong, I figure out why, and I rebuild the pattern.

Athletes are easy.

They come in with an acute thing.

Torn ACL, strained rotator cuff, stress fracture.

I fix the damage, I fix the pattern, I send them back.

4 to 8 weeks.

Done.

Gardeners are different.

About 6 years ago I started getting referrals from primary care doctors — women mostly, 55 to 70, sent over for "chronic lower back pain" or "shoulder issues."

Standard stuff.

Except when I watched them move, something didn't add up.

These women didn't have acute injuries.

They had cumulative damage.

Years of it.

Layered on top of itself like rings in a tree.

Their right side was compensating for their left.

Their lumbar was in chronic low-grade spasm.

Their right shoulder sat lower than their left.

And they all had the same answer when I asked what they do.

"I garden."

I heard that sentence maybe 40 times before I actually listened to it.

The patient who made me listen was a woman named Gail.

63 years old.

Retired school administrator.

Castle Rock, Colorado.

She'd been gardening for 28 years.

Her primary sent her to me for lower back pain.

He'd told her it was probably just age.

That's the answer they always get.

"It's just age."

It's not age.

data.caption: slumberlee.com
data.copy:
I fed my daughter every time she woke up because that was the only thing that worked, until I found out the reason she kept waking had nothing to do with hunger.

My daughters name is Ally and She's five months old and I love her more than I knew I could love anything.

But I have to be honest.

I hadn't slept more than an hour and a half in a row in weeks.

I'm not exaggerating. An hour and a half. That's the longest stretch I'd gotten. 

And every single time Ally woke up, the only thing that got her back down was feeding her. 

So I'd feed her. She'd fall asleep. Ninety minutes later, she'd wake up again. I'd feed her again. She'd fall asleep again.

All night. Every night. Rinse and repeat.

I would tell myself she was hungry. She had to be hungry. That's the only thing that made sense. 

She must’ve been going through a growth spurt and she needed more milk. It was developmental and It would pass.

Except she wasn't eating like she was starving she'd latch for two minutes, maybe three, and be asleep again.

And she wasn't taking a full feed

She was just using me to fall back asleep. I knew that. I knew it and I kept doing it anyway

Because the second I tried not to feed her she screamed and I was so tired, so completely broken, that I always caved.

Every single time.

And here's the thing that was making me feel insane.

Ally went down fine at bedtime. That was never the problem. I'd put her down awake at 7:30, she'd fuss for a few minutes, and she'd fall asleep on her own. 

No feeding. No rocking. She knew how to fall asleep.

So why couldn't she stay asleep?

I read everything. I tried everything. I downloaded the wake window app huckleberry.

And I adjusted her schedule. I tried not feeding her when she woke up and just rocking her instead. 

She screamed for forty minutes and I caved and fed her anyway and cried in the bathroom afterward because I felt like such a failure.

But the worst part was what was happening to me at night.

Last Tuesday my vet brought up "quality of life."

That's code for euthanasia.

He didn't say the word. They never do. He just said "I think we need to start having a conversation about quality of life going forward" and watched my face crumble across the exam table.

She's only 9.

We'd been on Apoquel for 16 months. $2,880 of my money. And she was WORSE than the day we started.

• Bleeding paws
• Patchy belly
• Crying in her sleep at 2am

The vet had upped the dose 3 times already and now we were here. Talking about whether she should keep being alive.

I drove home and sat in my driveway for 40 minutes.

I didn't go inside bc I couldn't look at her yet. She was going to wag her tail when I opened the door. She always wagged her tail. Even when her paws were bleeding. Even when she'd been crying all night.

She'd hear my keys and pick her head up off her bed and wag.

That's the part that broke me. That she was in so much pain and still tried to love me.

I'd tried EVERYTHING by then.

Apoquel was the first thing the vet put us on. $180 a month. Worked great for about 5 weeks. Then it just... stopped doing anything.

So we increased the dose.

From 16mg to 27mg twice a day.

That worked for another few weeks. Then nothing again.

And here's the part nobody warned me about.

When the Apoquel stopped working, the itching came back WORSE than before.

Like her body was making up for lost time.

I learned later there's actually a name for that. They call it rebound itching. It's a known thing. Vets just don't tell you.

We tried Cytopoint. $95 a shot, supposed to last 6 weeks. Lasted 3.

We tried switching her food. Salmon and sweet potato. Lamb and rice. Hydrolyzed protein.

The vet derm wanted us on a prescription food that cost $130 a bag and made her gain weight.

My 11-year-old daughter won the school’s "Kindness Award" on Friday—and by Monday, I found her in the bathroom cutting her own hair because the girls she was so kind to had convinced her she was ugly.

Her name is Chloe.

Straight-A student.

Never caused drama. Never got in trouble.

She was the girl who always invited the lonely kid to sit at her table.

I thought I was doing everything right.

I taught her to "use her words."

I taught her to "be the bigger person."

I didn’t realize I was systematically training her to be prey.

"Chloe, sweetheart, what happened? Why did you do this?"

data.copy:
I am going to say something that every cat owner watching their senior cat waste away needs to hear..

Your cat is not dying of old age.

She is starving. While she eats.

And I know this because I am a retired veterinarian who spent 40 years watching cats die. And then I watched my own cat die. The same way.

What I found when she passed still gives me nightmares.

Read every word of this. Before you make any permanent decisions.

My name is Susan Davis.

I am 74 years old.

I retired three years ago after 41 years as a shelter veterinarian at Crestwood Animal Rescue in rural Tennessee.

In those 41 years, I processed over 19,000 cats.

I have seven cats of my own right now. All rescues. The oldest is 18.

I know what a dying cat looks like. I have held thousands of them.

I thought I knew why they died.

I was wrong.

I want to tell you about Maple.

Maple was my 14-year-old Maine Coon. Enormous, heavy, muscular — the kind of cat you could feel coming when she jumped on the bed.

Two years before I retired, Maple started losing weight.

Not dramatically. Not overnight.

Just... less of her every month.

I pet her one morning and felt something I hadn't felt in years.

Her spine.

Clear as a ridge through her fur.

I ran every test on her that I would have run on any patient. Full bloodwork. Thyroid panel. Kidney values. Ultrasound.

But I was still convinced he had hyperthyroidism or kidney failure, which is what many owners and vets assume when a senior cat wastes away.

Everything came back normal.

"She's just getting older," I told myself.

I said that to cat owners every single week. I believed it.

But Maple kept eating. Ravenously. She'd finish her bowl and cry for more an hour later. She was following me into the kitchen every time the refrigerator opened. I had never seen her this hungry.

And she was wasting away.

I switched her food. Premium. High-calorie. The most expensive bag on the shelf.

She kept declining.

data.copy:
UPDATE: 10 weeks on normal food with hypothyroidism.
I have good news.
A lot of you have been asking me to come back and update what happened.
So here it is…
========
First — thank you to everyone who commented on my original post. Seriously. I was losing my mind and you all made me feel like I wasn't crazy.

So many of you were in the exact same trap. The "I'm doing everything my doctor says but my body keeps getting worse" trap.

Yeah. That one.

========

Quick background for anyone new:

My name is Lily and I have hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's).

For 4 years I took my Levothyroxine every single morning.

Never missed a day.

Set an alarm. Same time. Every morning.

Did everything they told me to do.

And I was still exhausted.

Every. Single. Day.

========

Not tired like a normal person is tired.

Tired in a way I couldn't explain to anyone who hadn't felt it.

Sleeping 10 hours and waking up feeling like I hadn't slept at all.

Dragging myself through the morning like I was moving through wet concrete.

Collapsing by 2pm.

Cancelling plans with friends because I had nothing left.

Sitting on the sofa at 7pm unable to explain to my husband why I couldn't just watch a film with him.

There was nothing left to give.

========

And the brain fog.

God. The brain fog.

Forgetting words mid-sentence. Just. Gone.

Standing in a room with no idea why I walked in there.

Reading the same paragraph four times and still not taking it in.

Losing my train of thought in meetings and just... hoping nobody noticed.

Forgetting the names of people I'd known for years.

Feeling like my brain was running on dial-up while everyone else had fibre broadband.

Still losing words in conversations.

data.copy:
Three boys lived through that crash and died waiting for a door.

I was on the truck that pulled up four minutes later.

The handles were dead because the hit took the power.

The one window already broken was the work of a friend with his bare hands.

We cut the rest open, and for three of them it didn't matter anymore.

The twenty-year-old by the mailbox kept saying there were three more boys in the car.

He said it like he had misplaced them and our crew could still go get them.

The borrowed T-shirt around his hands had already gone dark.

He kept stepping around my captain's arm.

Each time he pointed at the car, smoke slid low across the grass.

The back-door handle wore a black glove mark from the first officer's last pull.

I stepped off the engine with the Halligan in my right hand and crossed the yard.

The car sat sideways against the block wall with the nose folded into the engine bay.

The driver's door had a crease through it that ran right across the handle.

The passenger side was tight against the wall.

The back door on our side looked clean enough that a neighbor tried it before we got there.

That handle moved in his hand and did nothing.

The first officer on scene had pulled on it hard enough to leave his glove mark in the paint.

The car gave him nothing back.

The boys inside were not thrown around the road.

They were still inside the shell.

One boy was out because the left rear window was gone.

The glass from that window was spread across the curb like road salt.

The friend had broken that window before our engine reached the yard.

He kept lifting both wrapped hands toward the one broken window.

My captain put one hand on his shoulder and moved him behind the engine.

My name is Ray Calder.

I have been a firefighter and EMT for almost twenty years.

I have cut open cars in ditches, in driveways, on bridges, and in water up to my belt.

I have heard people scream from inside a car.

I have heard people stop screaming from inside a car.…

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

allowed_apps: BOGOS.io Free Gift Buy X Get Y
KB Back In Stock Restock Alert
Sticky Add To Cart Booster Pro
POWR Email Popup Sales Pop Ups
EG Auto Add to Cart Free Gift
SA Request a Quote, Hide Price
Zoorix Sticky Add To Cart Bar
Tada Pop up Spin Wheel Popups
Coupon X: Discount Code Pop Up
SC Back in Stock Restock Alert

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
